comment: Values approximate; verify against NASA sources.
notes: Code generated with AI assistance (Claude). Reviewed by team. areal_density_kg_m2 is an ALL-UP figure per square metre of body/tank wall (pi * d * L): it folds in skin, bulkheads, stringers, plumbing and wiring, so dry structure mass = wall area x areal density. max_q_pa is the dynamic pressure a rocket of the reference fineness (length/diameter) tolerates; the sim scales it with q_limit_model. cost_per_m2 is in millions of USD per square metre of wall.

q_limit_model.formula: q_limit = max_q_pa * clamp(reference_fineness / (length / diameter), min_factor, max_factor)
q_limit_model.source: MADE UP for gameplay. Captures the real trend that long, thin rockets bend more easily (bending moment grows with length, section stiffness with diameter). Reference fineness 12 is roughly Redstone / Thor class.

materials.name: Aluminium alloy
materials.description: Light and easy to work. The standard choice for 1960s tanks.
materials.source: Areal density CALIBRATED so a Redstone-class tank section (1.78 m x 12 m, 67 m2) weighs about 3.0 t dry. Max q is a MADE-UP limit set above the roughly 30-35 kPa max-Q that real aluminium launchers (Saturn, Titan) flew through. Bulk density is 2014/2219-type alloy (about 2.8 g/cc). Cost is made up.

materials.name: Stainless steel
materials.description: Heavy but tough and cheap. Shrugs off a rough ride through the air.
materials.source: MADE UP: 1.4x the aluminium areal density and about 1.7x its q limit, for a clear light-vs-strong trade-off. Note the real Atlas used very thin pressure-stabilised stainless steel and was LIGHTER than aluminium designs; the game deliberately uses a conventional thick-wall steel structure instead. Bulk density is 301 stainless (about 7.9 g/cc).

materials.name: Titanium alloy
materials.description: Nearly as strong as steel at close to aluminium weight. Eye-wateringly expensive.
materials.source: MADE UP ratios (0.85x aluminium mass, about 1.55x its q limit, 5x cost) based on the real high strength-to-weight ratio of Ti-6Al-4V (about 4.43 g/cc), which was used in 1960s pressure vessels and the Mercury/Gemini capsule structure.
